# @ratmath/chaos 0.3.0: full documentation

> Dynamical systems and chaos for RatMath: orbits, periodic points, bifurcations, Lyapunov exponents, fractals, maps of the plane and flows, exact or certified. From https://ratmath.com/chaos/, commit 76c9e37. Each page ends with a runnable example; in it, PRINT(...) prints.


---

Page: https://ratmath.com/chaos/index.html

@ratmath/chaos

## Chaos without rounding error

A chaotic map doubles every rounding error at each step, so after about fifty steps a floating-point orbit has no correct digit left and nothing warns you. Here an orbit is the true one, exactly or inside an interval, periodic points are algebraic numbers, and the parameters at which cycles are born or double are proven.

### What is here

### A first program

```js
import { logistic, lyapunov, bifurcationPoint, itinerary } from "@ratmath/chaos";

const f = logistic(4);                       // x → 4x(1 − x)
f.orbit("1/3", 3);                           // 1/3, 8/9, 32/81, 6272/6561: the true orbit
f.compare("1/10", 80).parted;                // 52: the step where doubles have no digit right
f.periodicPoints(2).map((p) => p.text);      // ["(5 − √5)/8", "(5 + √5)/8"]
lyapunov(f, "1/10", { steps: 300 }).value;   // an interval, along the true orbit
bifurcationPoint(logistic(), { parameter: "r", period: 2, near: [3.44, 0.44] }).parameter;   // 1 + √6, proven
itinerary(f, "1/10", 12);                    // "LLRLRRRLLRLR"
```

### Three kinds of answer

Exact. The orbit of a rational point under a polynomial map is a list of rationals, and it is the true orbit. A periodic point of a polynomial map is a root of fn(x)−x, an algebraic number, kept with its minimal polynomial.

Certified. An interval with rational ends, proven to contain the true value: a long orbit (exact rationals grow too fast to keep), a multiplier, a Lyapunov exponent along a true orbit, the parameter of a bifurcation. Ask for more digits and the interval narrows.

Estimated. A bifurcation diagram is a picture made from finitely many floating-point iterates, and its result says `kind: "estimated"`. So does anything stated about a limit that was only observed, such as the ratios that approach Feigenbaum's constant.

### Numbers in

Starting points and parameters are exact: a whole number, a fraction `"1/3"` or a decimal string `"3.2"`, which means 16/5. A JavaScript number that is not whole is refused, because `0.1` is not one tenth and the point of the library is that the orbit you get is the orbit of the number you typed.

### Fractals, automata and honest pixels

The same three kinds of answer carry over to pictures. An [iterated function system](https://ratmath.com/chaos/iterated-function-systems.html) with rational maps has exact stages and a dimension that is exact or certified; the chaos game that draws it is an estimate and says so. Whether a fraction lies in a [Cantor set](https://ratmath.com/chaos/cantor-sets.html) is decided exactly. [L-systems](https://ratmath.com/chaos/l-systems.html) count their symbols by matrix powers and draw at multiples of 30° in exact coordinates, and [cellular automata](https://ratmath.com/chaos/cellular-automata.html) are exact by nature. In a [Mandelbrot or Julia picture](https://ratmath.com/chaos/mandelbrot-and-julia.html) or a picture of [Newton basins](https://ratmath.com/chaos/newton-basins.html), every pixel is proved outside, proved inside, or left undecided.

### The plane and flows

In two dimensions and for differential equations the exact answers mostly run out, and proof takes over. [Periodic points of the Hénon map](https://ratmath.com/chaos/plane-maps.html) are each proven to exist, alone in a small box, with a list that is proven complete; where a coordinate can be eliminated they are algebraic numbers again. The [cat map and the horseshoe](https://ratmath.com/chaos/cat-map-and-horseshoe.html) are exact throughout. A [flow](https://ratmath.com/chaos/flows.html) is solved inside boxes that are proven to hold the true solution, which is enough to prove that a [periodic orbit](https://ratmath.com/chaos/periodic-orbits.html) of the Lorenz system exists, with its period and multipliers, and to find and classify every [equilibrium](https://ratmath.com/chaos/equilibria.html) in a region and the parameters where they change. The numbers under these proofs are doubles rounded outward, so they are fast; the statements are still theorems.

Pictures of all of this are in [@ratmath/graphics](https://ratmath.com/graphics/). The [RatMath Shelf](https://ratmath.com/shelf/) page lists what exists across all the libraries.

### Try it

```js
const f = logistic(4);
PRINT("true orbit of 1/3:", f.orbit("1/3", 4).join(", "));
const c = f.compare("1/10", 70);
for (const n of [10, 30, 50, 52, 60, 70]) PRINT(`step ${n}: float ${c.rows[n].float.toFixed(12)}  true ${c.rows[n].exact.low.toDecimal(12)}  correct digits ${c.rows[n].digits.toFixed(1)}`);
PRINT("the double has no correct digit from step", c.parted);
PRINT("period 2:", f.periodicPoints(2).map((p) => p.text).join(" and "));
const vdp = vanDerPol(1).periodicOrbit({ variable: "y", value: 0, direction: -1 }, { x: 2 });
PRINT("Van der Pol's limit cycle, proven:", vdp.stability, "period", vdp.period.low.toDecimal(9));
henon().periodicPoints(2, { x: [-2, 2], y: [-2, 2] }).map((p) => `(${p.point[0].low.toDecimal(8)}, ${p.point[1].low.toDecimal(8)}) ${p.stability}`)
```

Reference

## Everything in the library

Every export of `@ratmath/chaos`, with what it takes and what it returns. Numbers go in as whole numbers, fractions or decimal strings; a JavaScript number that is not whole is refused where an exact value is meant.

### Maps

| Export | What it does |

| map(formula, { variable, params, critical }) | A map of the line from a formula in analytic's notation. Returns an IteratedMap. |

| logistic(r = 4), tent(mu = 2), quadratic(c = -2) | The standard families rx(1−x), μ(21​−∣x−21​∣) and x2+c. |

| doubling(x0, { base }) | x↦2xmod1 on a rational, exactly: { orbit, preperiod, period, cycle, floatReachesZeroAt }. |

| IteratedMap | The class. Fields: text, variable, params, polynomial (coefficients, or null), tree. |

### Methods of a map

| Method | What it does |

| at(x), enclose(X, bits), float(x), derivativeAt(x) | One step: exact, as an interval, in doubles; and f′. |

| orbit(x0, n, { maxBits }) | The true orbit in rationals. See Orbits. |

| enclosedOrbit(x0, n, { digits, bits }) | The true orbit as intervals: { terms, bits, width }. |

| floatOrbit(x0, n), cobweb(x0, n) | The orbit in doubles; the corner points of a cobweb diagram. |

| compare(x0, n, { digits }) | Float beside true: { rows, parted }. |

| fixedPoints(), periodicPoints(n) | Exact points of least period n with multiplier and stability. See Periodic points. |

| cycles(n) | The points grouped into cycles, each with its multiplier and Lyapunov exponent. |

| periodicPointsIn(n, [a, b], { digits }) | Certified periodic points of any formula. |

| iterate(n), criticalPoints([a, b]), with(params) | fn as coefficients; zeros of f′; the family at other parameters. |

### Exponents, bifurcations, symbols

| Export | What it does |

| lyapunov(f, x0, { steps, transient, digits }) | The average of log\|f′\| along the true orbit, enclosed. See Lyapunov exponents. |

| lyapunovExponent(f, { distribution, interval, digits }), invariantDensity(f) | The exponent of almost every orbit as a certified integral of log\|f′\| against the invariant measure. See Lyapunov exponents. |

| sensitivity(f, x0, delta, { steps, threshold }) | The separation of two true orbits, step by step. |

| bifurcationPoint(family, { parameter, period, multiplier, near, digits }) | A parameter where a cycle's multiplier is ±1, proven. See Bifurcations. |

| periodDoubling(family, { parameter, levels, start }) | The cascade, each doubling proven, and the ratios of the gaps. |

| periodicWindow(family, { parameter, period, near }) | Birth, superstable parameter and first doubling of a window. |

| superstable(family, { parameter, period, range, critical }) | Parameters where the critical point has the given period. |

| bifurcationDiagram(family, { parameter, range, count, transient, keep }) | Data for the picture, in doubles, marked estimated. |

| itinerary(f, x0, n), kneading(f, n) | Symbol strings on true orbits. See Symbolic dynamics. |

| sharkovskii | { order(limit), compare(a, b), forces(a, b), forced(n, limit) }. |

| ChaosError | What the library throws, with a code: inexact, too-large, escapes, not-polynomial, not-proven and others. |

| plan | The phases still to come. Every phase is built, so the list is empty. |

### Maps of the plane

| Export | What it does |

| planeMap([f, g], { variables, params }), henon(a, b), standardMap(k), PlaneMap | A map of the plane from two formulas. Fields: text, variables, params, determinant (when constant), areaPreserving. See Maps of the plane. |

| at(p), float(p), enclose(P, bits), jacobian() | One step: exact, in doubles, as intervals; the Jacobian as formulas. |

| orbit, floatOrbit, enclosedOrbit, compare | As for maps of the line, on pairs. |

| periodicPoints(n, region, { all }), fixedPoints(region), cycles(n, region) | Every point of least period n in a box, each proven and alone in its enclosure, with multipliers and stability; complete says none was missed. |

| exactPeriodicPoints(n) | The points as algebraic numbers, when one coordinate can be eliminated. |

| lyapunov(p, n) | Both exponents, estimated; their sum enclosed when the determinant is constant. |

| catMap(), torusMap(matrix), TorusMap | Integer matrices on the torus, exact: at, orbit, period, periods(q), fixedPointCount(n), eigen(), entropy(), floatPartsAt. See The cat map and the horseshoe. |

| horseshoe(), Horseshoe | Smale's horseshoe in exact coordinates: at, itinerary, periodicPoint(word), periodicPoints(n), orbitCount(n), strips(n), dimension. |

### Flows

| Export | What it does |

| flow(field, { variables, params }), Flow | A system x′ = f(x) from one formula per variable. Fields: n, text, variables, params; with(params), jacobian(), velocity(p). |

| lorenz(s, r, b), rossler(a, b, c), vanDerPol(mu), pendulum(damping) | The standard systems. |

| solve(p0, until, { order, maxStep, maxSteps }) | The solution through a point or a box, enclosed: { final, complete, reason, reached, steps, width, at(t) }. See Flows. |

| floatOrbit(p0, until, { steps }) | A path in doubles for drawing: { t, points }. |

| returnMap(section, start, { returns }) | The return map of a section { variable, value, direction }: enclosures of the point, the time and the derivative. See Sections and periodic orbits. |

| periodicOrbit(section, guess, { returns, radius }) | A periodic orbit proven to exist near the guess, with period, multipliers and stability; or { proven: false, reason }. |

| equilibria(region) | Every equilibrium in a box, with eigenvalues and kind. See Equilibria. |

| bifurcations(param, [from, to], region, { samples, tol }) | Parameter brackets where equilibria appear, merge or change stability, named. |

### Fractals

| Export | What it does |

| new IFS(maps, { name, probabilities }), Affine | An iterated function system of affine maps with rational coefficients: stage(n), step, fixedPoint(i), contraction(), similarityDimension(), chaosGame(n, { seed }). See Iterated function systems. |

| attractors | sierpinski, carpet, vicsek, cantorDust, heighway, levyDragon, barnsley. |

| moran(ratios, { bits }) | The s with Σ rᵢ^s = 1: exact or certified. |

| boxCounting(points, { scales }), seeded(seed) | An estimated box dimension; a repeatable random generator. |

| cantor({ base, digits }) | A DigitCantor: contains(q), expansion(q), stage(n), measure(n), dimension(). See Cantor sets. |

| lsystem(spec), lsystems, LSystem, Q3 | L-systems: generate(n), counts(n), turtle(n). See L-systems. |

### Automata and pictures

| Export | What it does |

| elementary(rule), Elementary, showRows(rows) | Wolfram's rules: table, mirror, complement, equivalents, additive, step, run, fromCell, cycle. See Cellular automata. |

| life(cells, { rule }), Life, patterns | Life and its relatives on the unbounded plane: step, run, population, bounds, classify, toString. |

| mandelbrot(options), julia(c, options) | PixelGrid of proved inside / outside / undecided pixels. See Mandelbrot and Julia sets. |

| mandelbrotPoint(c), juliaPoint(c, z0) | One exact point: { verdict, reason, period or escape }. |

| newtonBasins(coefficients, options) | PixelGrid labelled by proved root. See Newton basins. |

| PixelGrid | width, height, kind, counts, at(i, j), toText(chars). |

### Try it

```js
// Every map method on one small example.
const f = logistic("7/2");
PRINT(String(f));
PRINT("at 1/2:", String(f.at("1/2")), " f′(1/2):", String(f.derivativeAt("1/2")), " float:", f.float(0.5));
PRINT("f² =", f.iterate(2).join(", "), "(coefficients, constant first)");
PRINT("fixed:", f.fixedPoints().map((p) => `${p.text} (${p.stability})`).join(", "));
PRINT("4-cycle:", f.cycles(4).map((c) => `${c.values.map((v) => v.toString(6)).join(" → ")} (${c.stability})`).join("; "));
const H = henon();
PRINT(String(H), " determinant", String(H.determinant));
PRINT("Hénon fixed points:", H.exactPeriodicPoints(1).map((p) => p.text[0]).join(" and "));
PRINT("Lorenz equilibria:", lorenz().equilibria({ x: [-20, 20], y: [-20, 20], z: [-1, 40] }).map((e) => e.kind).join(", "));
kneading(f, 16)
```

## Explore

Type a map and a starting point. The page draws the cobweb, lists the true orbit beside the floating-point one, and finds the periodic points. Further down: the Hénon map with its periodic points proven, flows with their equilibria, escape-time pictures with every pixel proved or left undecided, attractors, and cellular automata.

### A map and an orbit

Map f(x)
r
x₀
Steps

Use `r` as the parameter in the formula. Exact inputs only: `3.2` means 16/5. Try r = 3.2 (a 2-cycle), 3.5 (a 4-cycle), 3.83 (the period-3 window) and 4.

### Periodic points

Period

For a polynomial map these are exact algebraic numbers. The Lyapunov exponent in the first panel is the certified average along the true orbit.

### A map of the plane

a
b
Period

The Hénon map (x,y)↦(1−ax2+y, bx). The dots are a floating-point orbit, an estimate of the attractor. The marked points are the points of the chosen least period in the square from −2 to 2, each proven to exist and to be alone in its box. Try a = 1, b = 0.3, where a cycle of period 4 attracts.

### A flow

System
Time

The curve is a path in doubles, for the eye. The table is proven: every equilibrium in the box shown, with its kind read from enclosed eigenvalues.

### Escape-time pictures

Picture
c or p
Re
Im

Dark pixels are proved inside (or, for Newton, a colour per proved root), pale ones proved outside, and the accent colour marks undecided pixels, which gather on the boundary. For Newton, give the coefficients highest first, separated by commas: `1, 0, 0, -1` is z³ − 1. Try the Mandelbrot set on Re −3/4, −1/2 and Im 0, 1/4, or the Julia set of c = −0.12 + 0.75i.

### Attractors and automata

Attractor
Points

Elementary rule
Steps

The chaos game is an estimate drawn from floats, and the page says the dimension it would have; the automaton is exact.

### Try it

```js
// The page above, as code.
const f = map("r*x*(1 - x)", { params: { r: 4 } });
const c = f.compare("1/10", 60);
PRINT("parted at step", c.parted);
PRINT("exponent over 60 steps:", lyapunov(f, "1/10", { steps: 60 }).value.low.toDecimal(8));
PRINT("logistic period 2:", f.periodicPoints(2).map((p) => `${p.text}: ${p.stability}`).join("; "));
PRINT("Hénon period 2:", henon().periodicPoints(2, { x: [-2, 2], y: [-2, 2] }).map((p) => `(${p.point[0].low.toDecimal(6)}, ${p.point[1].low.toDecimal(6)}) ${p.stability}`).join("; "));
lorenz().equilibria({ x: [-20, 20], y: [-20, 20], z: [-1, 40] }).map((e) => `(${e.point.map((c) => c.low.toDecimal(4)).join(", ")}) ${e.kind}`)
```

Page: https://ratmath.com/chaos/orbits.html

Topic

## Orbits, true and floating

Iterating a map is the whole subject, and it is the one computation floating point cannot be trusted with. An orbit here comes in three kinds, and they can be put side by side.

```js
const f = logistic(4);              // or map("r*x*(1 - x)", { params: { r: 4 } })
f.orbit("1/3", 3);                  // exact rationals
f.enclosedOrbit("1/10", 200);       // { terms, bits, width }: the true orbit as intervals
f.floatOrbit(0.1, 200);             // what a program computes
f.compare("1/10", 80);              // { rows, parted }
doubling("1/10");                   // x → 2x mod 1 on a rational, with its cycle
```

### The exact orbit

If f is a polynomial with rational coefficients and x0​ is rational, every xn​=f(xn−1​) is rational and `orbit` returns them. This is the true orbit, but it cannot be long: for a quadratic map the number of digits doubles at every step, so x20​ already has about a million. `orbit` stops with an error once a term passes `maxBits` binary digits.

### The enclosed orbit

For long orbits each term is kept as an interval [an​,bn​] with rational ends that is certain to contain the true xn​. The next interval is computed so that it contains f(x) for every x in the current one, and its ends are rounded outward to a fixed number of binary digits. Chaos stretches intervals too: with a Lyapunov exponent λ the width grows like eλn. The cure is to carry more digits than the stretching eats, and `enclosedOrbit` does that itself: it starts again with twice the digits until the last term is known to the accuracy asked for. For the logistic map with r = 4, one binary digit is lost per step, so 200 steps to 12 decimals needs about 250 binary digits. The result reports the number it used.

An orbit that runs off to infinity is reported as such, and an interval that reaches a division by zero is refused.

### The floating-point orbit, and where it parts

A double has 53 binary digits. Each step of a chaotic map magnifies the rounding error of the step before, so the float orbit drifts from the true one and, after roughly 53/(λ/ln 2) steps, has nothing in common with it. `compare` returns both, with the error and the number of correct digits at every step, and `parted`, the first step at which no digit is right. The float orbit still looks like an orbit of the map, which is why the failure is invisible without the true one beside it.

### The doubling map

x↦2xmod1 shifts the binary expansion of x one place to the left. A rational p/q has a repeating expansion, so its orbit is eventually periodic, and `doubling` finds the cycle exactly. In doubles every number has a finite binary expansion, so every float orbit reaches 0 within about 55 steps and stays there: the computed behaviour is wrong for every starting point that does not really end at 0. `floatReachesZeroAt` gives the step.

| call | returns |

| map(formula, { variable = "x", params }) | IteratedMap |

| logistic(r), tent(mu), quadratic(c) | rx(1−x), μ(21​−∣x−21​∣), x2+c |

| f.at(x), f.enclose(X), f.float(x), f.derivativeAt(x) | Rational, RationalInterval, number |

| f.orbit(x0, n, { maxBits }) | Rational[] |

| f.enclosedOrbit(x0, n, { digits = 12 }) | { terms, bits, width } |

| f.floatOrbit(x0, n), f.cobweb(x0, n) | number[]; points of a cobweb diagram |

| f.compare(x0, n) | { rows: [{ n, float, exact, error, digits }], parted } |

| f.with({ r: "3.2" }) | the same family at another parameter |

| doubling(x0, { base = 2 }) | { orbit, preperiod, period, cycle, floatReachesZeroAt } |

### Try it

```js
const f = logistic(4);
PRINT("exact:", f.orbit("1/3", 5).join("  "));
PRINT("digits in the 12th term:", String(f.orbit("1/3", 12)[12].denominator).length);

const e = f.enclosedOrbit("1/10", 200, { digits: 15 });
PRINT(`x_200 = ${e.terms[200].low.toDecimal(15)}…  (width ${e.width.toNumber().toExponential(1)}, ${e.bits} binary digits carried)`);
PRINT("float x_200 =", f.floatOrbit(0.1, 200)[200], " which is unrelated");

const c = f.compare("1/10", 60);
for (const r of c.rows.filter((r) => r.n % 10 === 0)) PRINT(`n = ${r.n}: correct digits ${r.digits.toFixed(1)}`);
PRINT("parted at step", c.parted);

const d = doubling("1/10");
PRINT("doubling map from 1/10:", d.orbit.join(" → "), `then back to ${d.cycle[0]}; in doubles it is 0 from step ${d.floatReachesZeroAt}`);
tent(2).orbit("1/7", 6).join(" → ")
```

Page: https://ratmath.com/chaos/periodic-points.html

Topic

## Periodic points and stability

A point of period n satisfies fn(x)=x. For a polynomial map that is a polynomial equation, so its solutions are algebraic numbers and can be had exactly.

```js
logistic(4).fixedPoints();          // 0 and 3/4, with multipliers 4 and −2
logistic(4).periodicPoints(2);      // (5 ± √5)/8
logistic("3.2").cycles(2);          // one attracting 2-cycle, multiplier 4/25
map("sin(pi*x)").periodicPointsIn(1, [0, 1]);   // certified, for a map that is not a polynomial
```

### Least period

The roots of fn(x)−x include the points of every period dividing n. `periodicPoints(n)` removes them: it divides out the common factors with fd(x)−x for each proper divisor d, then asks `@ratmath/algebraic` for the real roots of what is left. Each comes back as an algebraic number: a fraction when it is rational, a closed form such as (5 − √5)/8 when it is quadratic, and otherwise its minimal polynomial with an interval that can be refined without limit.

### The multiplier

By the chain rule the derivative of fn is the same at every point of a cycle,

(fn)′(x0​)=f′(x0​)f′(x1​)⋯f′(xn−1​),
and this number, the multiplier, decides what nearby orbits do. If its absolute value is below 1 the cycle attracts them, above 1 it repels them. The multiplier is returned as an enclosure, and the stability is stated only when the enclosure settles it.

The borderline cases are where things change, so they are decided exactly. The multiplier is a polynomial in the root; it equals 1, −1 or 0 exactly when that polynomial minus the constant is divisible by the root's minimal polynomial, which is a finite computation with no rounding. A multiplier of exactly 0 is reported as `"superattracting"`, and of exactly ±1 as `"neutral"`: for r = 3 the fixed point 2/3 of the logistic map has multiplier −1, the moment of the first period doubling.

### Cycles

`cycles(n)` groups the points into orbits by applying f to each and seeing which point it lands on (the intervals are refined until that is unambiguous). Each cycle carries its Lyapunov exponent n1​log∣multiplier∣, which for a cycle is exact up to the enclosure of the logarithm.

### Maps that are not polynomials

For any formula, `periodicPointsIn(n, [a, b])` finds the zeros of fn(x)−x in an interval with analytic's certified zero finder: each returned interval is proven to contain exactly one. The multiplier is enclosed along the enclosed cycle.

| call | returns |

| f.fixedPoints(), f.periodicPoints(n) | [{ value, text, period, multiplier, stability, exactMultiplier }] |

| f.cycles(n) | [{ period, points, values, multiplier, stability, lyapunov }] |

| f.periodicPointsIn(n, [a, b], { digits }) | [{ value, period, leastPeriod, multiplier, stability }] |

| f.iterate(n) | the coefficients of fn, constant term first |

| f.criticalPoints([a, b]) | where f′ = 0 |

### Try it

```js
const f = logistic(4);
for (const p of f.fixedPoints()) PRINT(`fixed point ${p.text}: multiplier ${p.multiplier.low.toDecimal(6)}, ${p.stability}`);
for (const p of f.periodicPoints(2)) PRINT(`period 2: ${p.text}, multiplier ${p.multiplier.low.toDecimal(6)}`);
for (const c of f.cycles(3)) PRINT(`3-cycle ${c.points.join(" → ")}  multiplier ${c.multiplier.low.toDecimal(4)}  exponent ${c.lyapunov.low.toDecimal(10)} (ln 2 = ${Math.log(2).toFixed(10)})`);
PRINT("degree of the equation for period 3:", f.iterate(3).length - 1);

for (const r of ["2", "3", "3.2", "3.5"]) {
  const g = logistic(r);
  PRINT(`r = ${r}: fixed point ${g.fixedPoints()[1].text} is ${g.fixedPoints()[1].stability};`, "2-cycles:", g.cycles(2).map((c) => `${c.points.join(", ")} (${c.stability})`).join("; ") || "none");
}
map("sin(pi*x)").periodicPointsIn(1, [0, 1]).map((p) => `${p.value.low.toDecimal(12)} ${p.stability}`)
```

---

Page: https://ratmath.com/chaos/lyapunov.html

Topic

## Lyapunov exponents and sensitivity

Two orbits that start a distance δ apart are, after n steps, about δeλn apart. The number λ is the Lyapunov exponent, and a positive one is what "chaotic" means in practice.

```js
lyapunov(logistic(4), "1/10", { steps: 300 });           // { value, float, bits, kind }
lyapunov(logistic("3.2"), "1/10", { steps: 200, transient: 100 });
sensitivity(logistic(4), "1/10", "1/1000000000000");     // { rows, reaches, rate, factor }
```

### The definition

The distance between nearby orbits is multiplied at each step by about ∣f′(xi​)∣, so

λ=n→∞lim​n1​i=0∑n−1​log​f′(xi​)​.
`lyapunov` computes the average over `steps` terms (after discarding `transient`). What makes it different from the usual program is that the xi​ are the true orbit, enclosed with enough digits, and the logarithms are enclosed too, so the result is an interval that contains the finite-time average of the orbit you asked about. Its `kind` says so: certified for n steps. The limit itself is not something a finite computation proves, and for a chaotic orbit the average settles slowly as n grows.

The field `float` is the same average computed the ordinary way. For a chaotic orbit it differs from the certified one in the second or third decimal, because after fifty steps the program is averaging along a different orbit. Both are near the right answer for the same reason: almost every orbit gives the same limit.

### Where the value is known

- For an attracting cycle, λ is n1​log∣multiplier∣, negative, and cycles gives it directly. An orbit attracted to the cycle has the same exponent.

- For the tent map with slope 2, ∣f′∣=2 everywhere, so λ = ln 2 on every orbit.

- For the logistic map with r = 4, the change of variable x=sin2(πθ/2) turns it into the tent map, so λ = ln 2 for almost every starting point. Every periodic orbit except the fixed point 0 also has exactly ln 2 per step, as the 3-cycles on the previous page show.

### The limit itself: integrating against the invariant density

An orbit average over n steps is not the exponent, however large n is. But when the map has an ergodic invariant measure μ, almost every orbit spends its time according to μ, so the time average equals the space average:

λ=∫log∣f′(x)∣dμ(x).
For the logistic map at r=4 the measure is known. The change of variable x=sin2(πθ/2) turns 4x(1−x) into the tent map, which keeps length, so μ is the image of length: its distribution function is F(x)=π2​arcsinx​ and its density 1/(πx(1−x)​). `lyapunovExponent` encloses the integral, and the enclosure is a statement about the limit:

```js
const e = lyapunovExponent(logistic(4), { digits: 4 });
e.value;        // [0.69309…, 0.69317…], which contains log 2 = 0.693147…
e.invariance;   // { proven: true, reason: "x = sin(pi*θ/2)^2 turns the map into the tent map …", checks: […] }
```

The integrand is awkward twice over: the density is unbounded at 0 and 1, and log∣f′∣ is −∞ at the critical point 21​. The calculation is arranged so that neither needs a special rule.

- It works with F, which is continuous. The measure of a cell [l,r] is F(r)−F(l), and on a cell with midpoint m and g=log∣f′∣, ∫gdF=g(m)ΔF+g′(m)M1​+21​g′′(ξ)∫(x−m)2dF,M1​=2h​(F(l)+F(r))−∫lr​Fdx, where ∫(x−m)2dF lies in [0,h2/4]ΔF and ∫F lies between the midpoint and trapezoid rules wherever F is convex or concave.

- On a cell with the critical point c at one end, f′(x)=f′′(ξ)(x−c), so g=log∣f′′(ξ)∣+log∣x−c∣, and ∫0δ​logudu=δlogδ−δ is known exactly. The density is bounded there, and its range on the cell turns that into an interval.

Cells are halved where they contribute most to the width until the total is below the tolerance.

What is proven. The integral is enclosed for the measure given. That the measure is invariant is proven for the built-in maps by the change of variable named in `invariance.reason`. For a distribution you supply, it is tested: at several levels y the measure of {x:f(x)≤y} is computed from certified preimages and compared with F(y), and a mismatch is refused. The Chebyshev map 4x3−3x on [−1,1] with F=1−arccos(x)/π gives log3 this way. Ergodicity is taken from the theory of these maps and is stated in `note`.

### Sensitive dependence, measured

`sensitivity(f, x0, δ)` follows the true orbits of x0​ and x0​+δ together and returns their separation at each step as an enclosure, the first step at which it passes a threshold (1/10 by default), and the average growth factor per step up to then. For r = 4 the factor is about 2: a starting error of 10−12 is a visible error after about 36 steps, and no instrument or data type changes that count by much, since each extra decimal digit of accuracy buys only log2​10≈3.3 more steps.

| call | returns |

| lyapunov(f, x0, { steps = 200, transient = 0, digits = 10 }) | { value: RationalInterval, steps, transient, bits, kind, float } |

| lyapunovExponent(f, { distribution, interval, digits = 5 }) | { value: RationalInterval, distribution, density, criticalPoints, cells, invariance: { proven, reason, checks, holds }, exponent, note } |

| invariantDensity(f) | { density, distribution, interval, exponent, reason } for the logistic map at 4, the tent map at 2 and x² − 2 |

| sensitivity(f, x0, delta, { steps = 60, threshold = "1/10" }) | { rows: [{ n, separation }], reaches, rate, factor } |

### Try it

```js
const show = (iv) => iv.low.toDecimal(10);
const chaotic = lyapunov(logistic(4), "1/10", { steps: 300 });
PRINT("r = 4, 300 steps: certified", show(chaotic.value), " float", chaotic.float.toFixed(10), " ln 2 =", Math.log(2).toFixed(10));
PRINT("binary digits carried:", chaotic.bits);
PRINT("tent map:", show(lyapunov(tent(2), "1/7", { steps: 60 }).value));
const tame = lyapunov(logistic("3.2"), "1/10", { steps: 200, transient: 200 });
PRINT("r = 3.2 (attracting 2-cycle):", show(tame.value), " and log(4/25)/2 =", (Math.log(0.16) / 2).toFixed(10));

// The limit itself, from the invariant density: an enclosure of log 2.
const limit = lyapunovExponent(logistic(4), { digits: 3 });
PRINT("r = 4, from the density: [" + limit.value.low.toDecimal(6) + ", " + limit.value.high.toDecimal(6) + "]  with", limit.cells, "cells; invariance proven:", limit.invariance.proven);
PRINT("tent map, from the density:", show(lyapunovExponent(tent(2)).value));

const s = sensitivity(logistic(4), "1/10", "1/1000000000000", { steps: 50 });
for (const n of [0, 10, 20, 30, 36]) PRINT(`separation after ${n} steps: ${s.rows[n].separation.low.toNumber().toExponential(2)}`);
`passes 1/10 at step ${s.reaches}; grows by a factor ${s.factor.toFixed(3)} per step`
```

Page: https://ratmath.com/chaos/bifurcations.html

Topic

## Period doubling and windows

As the parameter of a family moves, attracting cycles appear, double and vanish. The parameters at which that happens are solutions of equations, and here each is proven to exist inside a tiny interval.

```js
const family = logistic();    // r is the parameter
bifurcationPoint(family, { parameter: "r", period: 1, near: [2.9, 0.6] });   // r = 3
periodDoubling(family, { parameter: "r", levels: 5, start: [2.9, 0.6] });    // 3, 3.449…, 3.544…, …
periodicWindow(family, { parameter: "r", period: 3, near: [3.835, 0.5] });   // born at 1 + √8
superstable(family, { parameter: "r", period: 2, range: [3, "7/2"] });       // 1 + √5
bifurcationDiagram(family, { parameter: "r", range: [2.8, 4], count: 400 }); // data for the picture (estimated)
```

### The two equations

A cycle of period n is a solution of g(x,r)=x with g=frn​. It changes its nature when its multiplier gx​(x,r) passes through ±1:

- −1: period doubling. The cycle stops attracting and an attracting cycle of period 2n splits off from it.

- +1: tangent bifurcation. A pair of cycles, one attracting and one repelling, appears out of nothing. This is how a periodic window opens in the middle of the chaotic range.

So a bifurcation is a solution (x, r) of two equations in two unknowns,

g(x,r)−x=0,gx​(x,r)=±1.
`bifurcationPoint` solves them in two stages. Newton's method in doubles finds an approximate solution near the point you give. Then Krawczyk's test is run in exact interval arithmetic on a small box B around it: if the interval Newton image K(B) lies strictly inside B, there is exactly one solution in B. That is a proof, and the box is then contracted until the parameter is known to the digits asked for. The derivatives of fn that the test needs come from the chain rule, carried through the n steps alongside the orbit.

### The cascade

`periodDoubling` follows the attracting cycle from one doubling to the next and proves each: for the logistic family r1​=3, r2​=1+6​, r3​=3.544090…, and so on. The gaps shrink by a factor that approaches Feigenbaum's constant δ = 4.669201609…, the same for every family with a quadratic maximum. The parameters are certified, and so is each ratio (rk​−rk−1​)/(rk+1​−rk​) as a quotient of intervals. That the ratios converge to δ is a theorem with a long computer-assisted proof, and it is not proven by this function, which says so in its `kind`.

### Windows and superstable cycles

`periodicWindow` returns the birth (multiplier +1) and the first doubling (multiplier −1) of an attracting cycle of the given period, both proven, and the parameter between them at which the cycle is superstable: it passes through the critical point, so its multiplier is 0. The period-3 window of the logistic family opens at 1+8​=3.828427… and its 3-cycle doubles at 3.841499…. By [Sharkovskii's theorem](https://ratmath.com/chaos/symbolic-dynamics.html), from that parameter on there are cycles of every period.

`superstable` finds every parameter in a range at which the critical point has period n. That is one equation in one unknown, frn​(c)=c, solved by the certified zero finder.

### The diagram

`bifurcationDiagram` gives the data for the familiar picture: for each parameter, the points an orbit visits after a transient. It is computed in doubles and labelled `kind: "estimated"`. It is a good picture, since the attractor a float orbit settles on is the right one even though the orbit is not, but it proves nothing, and it shows a cycle of high period and chaos identically.

| call | returns |

| bifurcationPoint(family, { parameter, period = 1, multiplier = -1, near: [r, x], digits = 20 }) | { parameter, point, period, multiplier, kind } |

| periodDoubling(family, { parameter, levels = 4, start: [r, x] }) | { points, parameters, ratios, feigenbaum, kind } |

| periodicWindow(family, { parameter, period, near: [r, x] }) | { period, born, doubles, superstable, width } |

| superstable(family, { parameter, period, range, critical }) | RationalInterval[] |

| bifurcationDiagram(family, { parameter, range, count, transient, keep }) | { kind: "estimated", columns: [{ parameter, points }] } |

### Try it

```js
const family = logistic();
const show = (iv, d = 15) => iv.low.toDecimal(d);
const d = periodDoubling(family, { parameter: "r", levels: 6, start: [2.9, 0.6] });
d.parameters.forEach((r, k) => PRINT(`period ${2 ** k} doubles at r = ${show(r)}   (width ${r.high.subtract(r.low).toNumber().toExponential(1)})`));
PRINT("1 + √6 =", (1 + Math.sqrt(6)).toFixed(15));
PRINT("ratios of the gaps:", d.ratios.map((q) => show(q, 6)).join(", "), " → δ =", d.feigenbaum);

const w = periodicWindow(family, { parameter: "r", period: 3, near: [3.835, 0.5] });
PRINT(`period-3 window: born ${show(w.born, 12)} (1 + √8 = ${(1 + Math.sqrt(8)).toFixed(12)}), superstable ${show(w.superstable, 12)}, doubles ${show(w.doubles, 12)}`);
PRINT("superstable 2-cycle at r =", show(superstable(family, { parameter: "r", period: 2, range: [3, "7/2"] })[0], 12), "= 1 + √5");

const pic = bifurcationDiagram(family, { parameter: "r", range: [2.8, 3.6], count: 9 });
pic.columns.map((c) => `r = ${c.parameter.toFixed(1)}: ${c.points.length > 16 ? "many" : c.points.length} point(s)`)
```

---

Page: https://ratmath.com/chaos/symbolic-dynamics.html

Topic

## Symbolic dynamics and Sharkovskii's order

Forget where the orbit is and record only which side of the turning point each term lies on. What is left is a string of letters, and a surprising amount of the dynamics can be read from it.

```js
itinerary(logistic(4), "1/10", 30);      // "LLRLRRRLLRLRRLLLLLLRRRRLLRLLRR"
kneading(logistic("3.83"), 12);          // "RLRRLRRLRRLR": the critical orbit is attracted to a 3-cycle
sharkovskii.order(12);                   // [3, 5, 7, 9, 11, 6, 10, 12, 8, 4, 2, 1]
sharkovskii.forces(3, 1000);             // true: period three implies every period
```

### Itineraries

For a map with one turning point c, write L if xn​<c, R if xn​>c and C if xn​=c. The string for the orbit of x0​ is its itinerary. Because f is increasing on one side of c and decreasing on the other, the itinerary determines the order of points on the line: two points with different itineraries can be told apart, and which is to the left can be read off from where the strings first differ and how many R's came before.

An itinerary is exactly the kind of thing floating point gets wrong: one misplaced term near c changes every later comparison. `itinerary` follows the true orbit, in exact rationals while they stay small and then with enclosures, adding digits whenever a term is too close to c to place. For the full logistic map (r = 4) and the tent map, the itinerary is the binary expansion of the starting point in disguise, which is why every string of L's and R's occurs.

### Kneading sequences

The itinerary of the critical value f(c) is the kneading sequence of the map. It is the largest itinerary any point can have (in the order above), so it describes which strings are allowed at all. As the parameter of the logistic family increases, the kneading sequence increases with it, and a periodic kneading sequence marks a superstable or attracting cycle: at r = 3.83, inside the period-3 window, it is RLR repeated.

### Sharkovskii's order

Order the positive whole numbers like this:

3▹5▹7▹⋯▹2⋅3▹2⋅5▹⋯▹4⋅3▹4⋅5▹⋯▹8▹4▹2▹1.
First the odd numbers from 3 up, then twice them, then four times them, and so on, and at the very end the powers of two going down. Sharkovskii's theorem says that a continuous map of an interval with a point of least period n has points of every least period that comes after n in this order. Period 3 is first, so it forces every period: "period three implies chaos". And a map with only finitely many periods has only powers of two, which is the period-doubling cascade seen from the other end.

`sharkovskii.compare(a, b)` is a comparison function for this order, `forces(a, b)` answers whether period a forces period b, and `forced(n, limit)` lists what a period forces.

| call | returns |

| itinerary(f, x0, n, { critical }) | a string of L, R and C |

| kneading(f, n, { critical }) | the itinerary of f(c) |

| sharkovskii.order(limit), .compare(a, b), .forces(a, b), .forced(n, limit) | |

### Try it

```js
PRINT("logistic r = 4 from 1/10:", itinerary(logistic(4), "1/10", 40));
PRINT("tent map from 1/7:      ", itinerary(tent(2), "1/7", 12), " (1/7 = 0.001001…₂ has period 3)");
for (const r of ["3.2", "3.5", "3.83", "3.9", "4"]) PRINT(`kneading sequence at r = ${r}:`, kneading(logistic(r), 24));
PRINT("Sharkovskii's order up to 20:", sharkovskii.order(20).join(" ▷ "));
PRINT("period 6 forces:", sharkovskii.forced(6, 20).join(", "));
PRINT("does 5 force 3?", sharkovskii.forces(5, 3), "  does 3 force 5?", sharkovskii.forces(3, 5));
// the period-3 window really does contain a point of period 5:
logistic("3.84").periodicPointsIn(5, ["0.1", "0.99"], { digits: 12 }).filter((p) => p.leastPeriod === 5).length + " points of period 5 at r = 3.84"
```

---

Page: https://ratmath.com/chaos/plane-maps.html

Topic

## Maps of the plane

A map of the plane takes a point (x,y) to another. Two formulas are enough for folding, stretching and a strange attractor. Orbits come exact, enclosed or in doubles as on the line, and periodic points are proven to exist, each alone in a small box.

```js
const H = henon();                        // (x, y) → (1 − 1.4x² + y, 0.3x)
H.orbit([0, 0], 3);                       // (0, 0), (1, 0), (−2/5, 3/10), (269/250, −3/25): the true orbit
H.compare([0, 0], 150).parted;            // 93: the step where doubles have no digit right
H.fixedPoints({ x: [-2, 2], y: [-1, 1] });        // two, each proven, and proven to be all
H.exactPeriodicPoints(1).map((p) => p.text);      // [["(−7 − √609)/28", …], ["(−7 + √609)/28", "(−21 + 3√609)/280"]]
planeMap(["x/2 + y/4 + 1", "x/4 - y/3"]);         // any two formulas
```

### The Hénon map

Hénon's map is the simplest map of the plane with a strange attractor:

H(x,y)=(1−ax2+y,bx),a=1.4, b=0.3.
It bends the plane (the x2 term), squeezes it (the Jacobian determinant is −b everywhere, so areas shrink by the factor 0.3 at every step) and flips it. `H.determinant` is that constant, found by expanding the determinant of the Jacobian symbolically, and `H.areaPreserving` is true when it is 1 or −1.

A rational starting point has a rational orbit, and `orbit` gives it. The number of digits doubles at each step, so long orbits are enclosed instead: `enclosedOrbit(p, n)` adds working digits until the last point is known to the accuracy asked for. `compare` sets the double orbit beside the true one. From (0,0) the doubles lose their last correct digit at step 93: the error doubles about every 1.6 steps, which is the Lyapunov exponent at work.

### Periodic points, proven

A point of period n is a solution of Fn(p)=p, two equations in two unknowns. `periodicPoints(n, region)` searches a rectangle by subdivision. A box is thrown away when interval arithmetic shows that Fn(p)−p cannot vanish in it. A box is kept as a solution when Krawczyk's test succeeds: with G=Fn−id, m the centre of the box X and C an approximate inverse of DG(m), if

K(X)=m−CG(m)+(I−CDG(X))(X−m)
lies in the interior of X, then G has exactly one zero in X, and it lies in K(X). So every point in the list exists and is the only one in its enclosure, and when the list's `complete` is true, the rest of the rectangle was proven empty. For the classical parameters the search finds 2 fixed points, one orbit of period 2, one of period 4, two of period 6 and four of period 7, and none of period 3 or 5.

Each point comes with the eigenvalues of DFn there (its multipliers), as enclosures, and a verdict: `attracting` (both inside the unit circle), `repelling`, `saddle`, or `elliptic` for a complex pair of an area-preserving map. At a saddle, `unstable` and `stable` are the eigenvectors: the directions along which nearby points leave and arrive. The unstable direction at the fixed point on the attractor is the direction of the attractor's leaves there.

### Periodic points, exact

For a polynomial map the equations are polynomial. When one of them is of first degree in one unknown, that unknown can be eliminated and the other is a root of a polynomial in one variable: an algebraic number. For the Hénon family this works for periods 1 and 2, and `exactPeriodicPoints(n)` returns the points in closed form:

x=2a−(1−b)±(1−b)2+4a​​,y=bx.
For higher periods neither equation is linear, and the method says so; the proven enclosures above remain.

### Lyapunov exponents

A map of the plane has two exponents: the growth rate of a tangent vector, and of an area. `lyapunov(p, n)` estimates both in doubles, re-orthogonalising two tangent vectors at each step, and labels the result `kind: "estimated"`. One thing about them is exact: their sum is the average of log∣detDF∣, and when the determinant is constant that is log∣b∣. The result's `sum` is an enclosure of it, and the two estimates can be checked against it.

### The standard map

Chirikov's standard map models a kicked rotor,

y′=y+2πk​sin(2πx),x′=x+y′,
and keeps areas for every k: its determinant comes out as exactly 1, with the sines and cosines treated as symbols. `standardMap(k)` is the map lifted to the plane (take x and y modulo 1 to draw it on the torus). It has no rational orbits, so orbits are enclosed. Its fixed point at the origin is a saddle and the one at (21​,0) is elliptic for 0: the centre of the island that the pictures show.

| call | returns |

| planeMap([f, g], { variables, params }) | PlaneMap |

| henon(a = "1.4", b = "0.3"), standardMap(k = 1) | PlaneMap |

| F.at(p), F.float(p), F.enclose(p) | the image: exact, in doubles, enclosed |

| F.orbit(p, n), F.floatOrbit(p, n), F.enclosedOrbit(p, n, { digits }) | orbits of the three kinds |

| F.compare(p, n) | { rows: [{ n, float, exact, error, digits }], parted } |

| F.jacobian(), F.determinant, F.areaPreserving | formulas; a Rational or null; a boolean |

| F.periodicPoints(n, region, { all }) | [{ point, period, leastPeriod, multipliers, stability, stable, unstable }] with .complete |

| F.fixedPoints(region), F.cycles(n, region) | the same for n = 1; points grouped into orbits |

| F.exactPeriodicPoints(n) | [{ x, y, text, period, multipliers, stability }] |

| F.lyapunov(p, n) | { exponents, kind: "estimated", sum } |

### Try it

```js
const H = henon();
const show = (iv) => iv.low.toDecimal(10);
PRINT("true orbit of (0, 0):", H.orbit([0, 0], 4).map((p) => `(${p.join(", ")})`).join("  "));
PRINT("doubles have no correct digit from step", H.compare([0, 0], 150).parted);
const region = { x: [-2, 2], y: [-1, 1] };
for (const n of [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7]) {
  const pts = H.periodicPoints(n, region);
  PRINT(`least period ${n}: ${pts.length} points, ${pts.length / n} orbits${pts.complete ? ", proven to be all" : ""}`);
}
const p = H.fixedPoints(region)[1];
PRINT("fixed point on the attractor:", p.point.map(show).join(", "), " ", p.stability);
PRINT("  multipliers", p.multipliers.map((e) => show(e.re)).join(" and "));
PRINT("  unstable direction (1, " + show(p.unstable[1]) + "), stable direction (" + show(p.stable[0]) + ", 1)");
PRINT("exactly:", H.exactPeriodicPoints(1)[1].text.join(", "));
const l = H.lyapunov([0, 0], 20000);
PRINT("exponents (estimated):", l.exponents.map((x) => x.toFixed(4)).join(", "), " sum", (l.exponents[0] + l.exponents[1]).toFixed(6));
`log 0.3 = ${show(l.sum)}, the sum exactly`
```

---

Page: https://ratmath.com/chaos/cat-map-and-horseshoe.html

Topic

## The cat map and the horseshoe

Two maps of the plane can be done with no approximation at all, and they are the two that explain the rest: the cat map, where chaos is linear algebra, and the horseshoe, where it is counting words.

```js
const cat = catMap();                       // (x, y) → (2x + y, x + y) mod 1
cat.period(["3/101", "7/101"]).period;      // 25: every rational point is periodic
cat.floatPartsAt(["3/101", "7/101"]);       // 38: the step at which doubles have lost that orbit
cat.fixedPointCount(5);                     // 121n points fixed by the fifth iterate
cat.entropy().text;                         // "log((3 + √5)/2)"

const hs = horseshoe();
hs.periodicPoint("011");                    // [9/13, 3/13], the point whose itinerary is 011011011…
hs.orbitCount(6);                           // 9 orbits of least period 6
```

### The cat map

Arnold's cat map acts on the torus, the unit square with opposite sides glued:

(xy​)↦(21​11​)(xy​)mod1.
The matrix has whole entries and determinant 1, so the map is invertible and keeps areas. Its eigenvalues are λ=23+5​​≈2.618 and 1/λ: every small disc is stretched by λ along one direction and squeezed along the other, at every point, in the same directions. `eigen()` gives the eigenvalues and the slopes of the two directions as exact numbers in Q(5​); the slopes are irrational, which is why the stretched disc winds densely round the torus instead of closing up.

Rational points. A point with coordinates i/q,j/q goes to another such point, and there are only q2 of them, so (the map being invertible) every rational point is periodic. `period(p)` finds the period by exact iteration and `periods(q)` tabulates all points of denominator q. These are the famous pictures of a cat that reassembles after a few hundred steps: the pixels are rational points.

What doubles do. The same orbit in doubles is not periodic. Each step multiplies the rounding error by λ, so after n steps an error of 10−16 has grown to 10−16λn, which reaches the size of the torus near n=38. `floatPartsAt` reports that step. The true orbit of (3/101,7/101) returns after 25 steps for ever; the double orbit never returns.

Counting. The fixed points of the n-th iterate are the solutions of (An−I)p≡0, and there are exactly ∣det(An−I)∣ of them: 1, 5, 16, 45, 121, … (`fixedPointCount`). They grow like λn, and the growth rate logλ is the map's topological entropy and its Lyapunov exponent, which `entropy()` returns as a formula and an enclosure.

`torusMap(matrix)` takes any 2 × 2 matrix of whole numbers; `hyperbolic` says whether it has an eigenvalue on the unit circle (a rotation by a quarter turn does, and is not chaotic).

### The horseshoe

Smale's horseshoe takes a square, squeezes it to a third of its width, stretches it to three times its height, folds it and lays it back over the square. In the piecewise linear form used here,

H(x,y)={(x/3,3y)(1−x/3,3−3y)​y≤1/3(symbol 0)y≥2/3(symbol 1)​
and a point with 1/3 leaves the square. The points that stay for n steps form 2n horizontal strips (`strips(n)`), the stages of the middle-thirds Cantor set; the points that have been in the square for the last n steps form 2n vertical strips. The points that never leave in either direction are a product of two Cantor sets, of dimension 2log2/log3.

Symbolic dynamics. Write 0 or 1 according to which strip the point is in at each step. Every sequence of 0s and 1s is the itinerary of exactly one point of the invariant set, and applying H shifts the sequence. So the horseshoe contains, exactly:

- a periodic point for every periodic sequence: periodicPoint("011") solves the affine fixed-point equation along the word and returns a rational point; there are 2n points fixed by Hn, and orbitCount(n) orbits of least period n (2, 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, …);

- orbits that come arbitrarily close to every point of the set (take a sequence that contains every finite word);

- sensitive dependence: two points whose sequences first differ at step n are in different strips at step n.

The horseshoe matters because it is found inside other systems. Wherever a map stretches and folds a region across itself, a horseshoe sits inside, and with it all of the above. The saddle periodic orbits of the [Hénon map](https://ratmath.com/chaos/plane-maps.html) and of the [Lorenz system](https://ratmath.com/chaos/periodic-orbits.html) on the neighbouring pages are the visible part of such sets.

| call | returns |

| catMap(), torusMap(matrix) | TorusMap |

| T.at(p), T.orbit(p, n), T.floatOrbit(p, n) | exact points of the torus; doubles |

| T.period(p) | { period, preperiod, cycle } |

| T.periods(q) | Map from period to the number of points of denominator q with it |

| T.fixedPointCount(n) | bigint, \|det(Aⁿ − I)\| |

| T.eigen() | [{ value, text, direction, directionText, expanding }] |

| T.entropy() | { text, value: RationalInterval } |

| T.floatPartsAt(p) | the step at which the double orbit has left the true one |

| horseshoe() | Horseshoe |

| S.at(p), S.itinerary(p, n) | the image or null; a string of 0s and 1s |

| S.periodicPoint(word), S.periodicPoints(n), S.orbitCount(n) | exact points; all 2ⁿ with word and least period; a count |

| S.strips(n), S.dimension | exact intervals; { text, value } |

### Try it

```js
const cat = catMap();
PRINT(String(cat));
PRINT("orbit of (1/5, 2/5):", cat.orbit(["1/5", "2/5"], 3).map((p) => `(${p.join(", ")})`).join(" "));
PRINT("period of (3/101, 7/101):", cat.period(["3/101", "7/101"]).period, "  doubles lose it at step", cat.floatPartsAt(["3/101", "7/101"]));
PRINT("periods of the points with denominator 10:", [...cat.periods(10)].map(([p, k]) => `${k} of period ${p}`).join(", "));
PRINT("fixed points of the n-th iterate:", [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8].map((n) => cat.fixedPointCount(n)).join(", "));
for (const e of cat.eigen()) PRINT(`eigenvalue ${e.text}, direction of slope ${e.directionText}, ${e.expanding ? "expanding" : "contracting"}`);
PRINT("entropy", cat.entropy().text, "=", cat.entropy().value.low.toDecimal(15));

const hs = horseshoe();
for (const w of ["0", "1", "01", "011", "0010111"]) {
  const p = hs.periodicPoint(w);
  PRINT(`word ${w}: point (${p.join(", ")}), itinerary ${hs.itinerary(p, 14)}`);
}
PRINT("orbits of least period 1 to 10:", Array.from({ length: 10 }, (_, i) => hs.orbitCount(i + 1)).join(", "));
PRINT("strips after 2 steps:", hs.strips(2).horizontal.map(([a, b]) => `[${a}, ${b}]`).join(" "));
`dimension of the invariant set: ${hs.dimension.text} = ${hs.dimension.value.toFixed(6)}`
```

---

Page: https://ratmath.com/chaos/flows.html

Topic

## Flows, enclosed

A flow is the motion defined by a system of differential equations x′=f(x). On a chaotic flow a numerical solver drifts off the true solution like a float orbit does, only more quietly. Here the solution is enclosed: boxes that are proven to contain it, for a point or for a whole box of starting points.

```js
const L = lorenz();                            // x′ = 10(y − x), y′ = x(28 − z) − y, z′ = xy − (8/3)z
const s = L.solve([1, 1, 1], 20);
s.final;                                       // three intervals, each about 10⁻⁶ wide, that hold x(20), y(20), z(20)
s.at("7/2");                                   // the same at any earlier time
L.floatOrbit([1, 1, 1], 20, { steps: 2000 });  // Runge–Kutta: ends at 13.47…, but the true x(20) is 13.7931…
flow(["y", "-x - y^3"], { variables: ["x", "y"] });   // any formulas
```

### The systems

- lorenz(s, r, b): x′=s(y−x), y′=x(r−z)−y, z′=xy−bz, by default 10, 28, 8/3: Lorenz's model of convection and the first strange attractor.

- rossler(a, b, c): x′=−y−z, y′=x+ay, z′=b+z(x−c): one nonlinear term, and a band that folds once.

- vanDerPol(mu): x′=y, y′=μ(1−x2)y−x: an oscillator that settles on one limit cycle whatever the start.

- pendulum(c): x′=y, y′=−sinx−cy.

- flow(formulas, { variables, params }) for anything else built from + − × ÷, whole powers, sin and cos. Parameters are exact numbers, and with({ r: 24 }) gives the same family at other values.

### How the solution is enclosed

The solver takes steps. In one step of length h from a set of points:

- A rough box. A box R with X+[0,h]f(R)⊆R contains the solution on the whole step, by the Picard–Lindelöf theorem.

- A Taylor polynomial with a bounded remainder. The Taylor coefficients of the solution are computed from the formulas by automatic differentiation, in interval arithmetic. The polynomial of degree 12 from the centre of the set is the main part; the next coefficient, taken over all of R, bounds what was left out.

- The derivative of the flow. The same is done for the variational equation V′=Df(x)V, which gives an interval matrix A containing the derivative of the time-h map at every point of the set. By the mean value theorem the image of the set lies in (image of the centre) + A·(set − centre).

- Sets that turn. A set is kept as a centre, a frame and a box of coordinates in that frame, and the new frame is the orthogonal factor of A times the old one (Lohner's method). A box with fixed axes would be re-wrapped at every step and grow even on a rigid rotation; a frame that turns with the flow does not.

All arithmetic is in doubles rounded outward, so the bounds are bounds, and since a double is an exact rational the results are handed back as `RationalInterval`s. The sine and cosine come from their own series with the remainder bounded, not from the platform's.

### What it shows on a chaotic flow

From (1,1,1) the Lorenz solution is enclosed to within 10−9 at t=10, 10−6 at t=20 and 0.04 at t=30: the enclosure widens at the rate the flow separates orbits (the Lyapunov exponent is about 0.9, so a factor of e9≈8000 per ten time units), because rounding errors are perturbations too and the enclosure has to hold them all. That widening is the honest part. A Runge–Kutta solver with 2000 steps returns x(20)=13.47 with nothing to say that only the first two digits are right; the enclosure shows 13.7931.

The same widening limits how far a set can be followed. A box of starting points of width w picks up an error of order w2 per step from the curvature of the flow, so thin sets go far and wide ones do not. When no enclosure can be found the solver stops and says where: `complete` is false, `reached` is the time it got to, and `reason` says why. A solution that blows up in finite time, such as x′=x2 from 1, ends that way just before t=1.

For a single orbit to many digits there is also analytic's `ode.solve`, which works in exact rational arithmetic with Taylor models. It is some hundred times slower, and it is what to use when 15 digits are not enough.

| call | returns |

| flow(formulas, { variables, params }) | Flow |

| lorenz(s, r, b), rossler(a, b, c), vanDerPol(mu), pendulum(c) | Flow |

| F.solve(p0, until, { order = 12, maxStep, maxSteps }) | { final, at(t), complete, reason, reached, steps, width } |

| F.floatOrbit(p0, until, { steps }) | { t, points } by Runge–Kutta in doubles |

| F.with(params), F.jacobian(), F.velocity(p) | the family at other parameters; formulas; the field in doubles |

### Try it

```js
const L = lorenz();
PRINT(String(L));
const wide = (s) => s.width.toExponential(1);
for (const T of [5, 10, 20]) {
  const s = L.solve([1, 1, 1], T);
  PRINT(`t = ${T}: x in [${s.final[0].low.toDecimal(8)}, ${s.final[0].high.toDecimal(8)}], width ${wide(s)}, ${s.steps} steps`);
}
for (const steps of [2000, 20000]) PRINT(`Runge–Kutta, ${steps} steps: x(20) = ${L.floatOrbit([1, 1, 1], 20, { steps }).points.at(-1)[0].toFixed(8)}`);

const box = flow(["-x"]).solve([[1, 2]], 1);
PRINT("x′ = −x from the box [1, 2] to t = 1:", box.final[0].low.toDecimal(8), "to", box.final[0].high.toDecimal(8), " (1/e and 2/e)");
const up = flow(["x^2"]).solve([1], 2);
PRINT("x′ = x² from 1: complete", up.complete, " reached t =", up.reached.low.toDecimal(4));
const P = pendulum().solve(["1/2", 0], 10);
`pendulum from angle 1/2 at t = 10: ${P.final[0].low.toDecimal(11)}, width ${wide(P)}`
```
