Page: https://ratmath.com/chaos/periodic-orbits.html

Topic

## Sections and periodic orbits

Cut a flow with a plane and watch where orbits come back to it: the flow becomes a map, and a periodic orbit becomes a fixed point. Because the return map and its derivative are enclosed, the fixed point can be proven to exist. That turns a closed curve on a screen into a theorem.

```js
const V = vanDerPol(1);
const section = { variable: "y", value: 0, direction: -1 };      // y = 0, crossed with y decreasing
V.returnMap(section, { x: 2 });               // { point: [2.0086122778…], time: 6.65156…, derivative: [[0.00089996…]] }
const orbit = V.periodicOrbit(section, { x: 2 });
orbit.proven;                                 // true
orbit.period;                                 // 6.66328685932…, an interval 10⁻¹² wide
orbit.stability;                              // "attracting"

lorenz().periodicOrbit({ variable: "z", value: 27 }, { x: -13.76, y: -19.58 }, { returns: 2 });
// proven: a saddle orbit of period 1.558652210…, expanding by 4.7129 each time round
```

### The return map

A section is a plane {xj​=v} with a direction of crossing: `{ variable: "z", value: 27, direction: 1 }` means the plane z=27 crossed with z increasing. Its points are named by the other variables. The first-return map P sends a point of the section to the next point where its orbit crosses the section in the same direction.

`returnMap(section, start)` follows a point, or a box of points given as intervals, and returns enclosures of P, of the time taken, and of the derivative DP in the section's coordinates. On the way the solver watches every step for crossings: a step whose rough box meets the plane must have the field pointing strictly through it, so each crossing is counted once and in the right direction; if the field might be tangent to the section there, the call stops and says so. At the crossing itself each point of the set is moved along the field onto the plane, which gives

DP=(I−fj​fejT​​)Dφτ​,
the derivative of the flow with the direction of the flow projected out. `returns: k` gives the k-th return.

### Proving a periodic orbit

A periodic orbit crosses the section at a fixed point of P (or of Pk). `periodicOrbit(section, guess)` first improves the guess by Newton's method on P(x)−x, using the enclosed return map as a very accurate numerical one. Then it takes a small box X round the candidate m and applies Krawczyk's test to G(x)=P(x)−x:

K(X)=m−CG(m)+(I−C(DP(X)−I))(X−m)⊂intX.
When the inclusion holds, P has exactly one fixed point in X: a periodic orbit exists, it crosses the section inside the box returned as `point`, and no other periodic orbit of that many returns crosses within `radius` of it. The test needs DP−I to be invertible, so it works for attracting, repelling and saddle orbits alike; it does not work at an orbit with a multiplier equal to 1, and there the result has `proven: false` and a reason.

The eigenvalues of DP at the fixed point are the orbit's multipliers (Floquet multipliers): all inside the unit circle for an attracting cycle, on both sides for a saddle.

### Three orbits

Van der Pol. The limit cycle for μ=1 crosses y=0 at x=2.00861986087… with period 6.66328685932…, and the return map contracts by the factor 0.00086 there: after one turn a nearby orbit is a thousand times closer.

Rössler. For c=2.5 the attractor is a single cycle, proven attracting. For the classical c=5.7 the attractor is chaotic, and the orbit that turns once is still there inside it, as a saddle with multiplier −2.40: the minus sign says that the band it lives on is twisted like a Möbius strip.

Lorenz. The attractor contains infinitely many periodic orbits, all of them saddles, and none can be found by waiting for an orbit to settle. The shortest winds once round each wing. It crosses z=27 upward twice per period, so it is a fixed point of the second return: `{ returns: 2 }`. Its period, 1.5586522107…, agrees with the value computed by Viswanath to many more digits, and here it is the period of an orbit that provably exists.

| call | returns |

| F.returnMap(section, start, { returns = 1 }) | { variables, point, time, derivative }, all enclosures |

| F.periodicOrbit(section, guess, { returns = 1, radius }) | { proven: true, point, period, multipliers, stability, radius } or { proven: false, point, reason } |

| section | { variable, value = 0, direction = 1 }: direction 1 or "up", −1 or "down" |

### Try it

```js
const show = (iv, n = 11) => iv.low.toDecimal(n);
const tell = (name, o) => {
  if (!o.proven) return PRINT(name, "not proven:", o.reason);
  PRINT(`${name}: proven, ${o.stability}`);
  PRINT(`  crosses at (${o.point.map((x) => show(x, 9)).join(", ")}), period ${show(o.period)}`);
  PRINT(`  multipliers ${o.multipliers.map((e) => e.re.high.toNumber().toPrecision(5)).join(", ")}`);
};
const down = { variable: "y", value: 0, direction: -1 };
const V = vanDerPol(1);
const r = V.returnMap(down, { x: 2 });
PRINT("Van der Pol, one return from x = 2:", show(r.point[0]), "after time", show(r.time, 8), " derivative", r.derivative[0][0].low.toDecimal(8));
tell("Van der Pol, μ = 1", V.periodicOrbit(down, { x: 2 }));
tell("Rössler, c = 2.5", rossler("0.2", "0.2", "2.5").periodicOrbit(down, { x: -3.7, z: 0.03 }));
tell("Rössler, c = 5.7", rossler().periodicOrbit(down, { x: -7.2, z: 0.02 }));
tell("Lorenz, once round each wing", lorenz().periodicOrbit({ variable: "z", value: 27 }, { x: -13.76, y: -19.58 }, { returns: 2 }));
tell("a damped oscillator", flow(["y", "-x - y"]).periodicOrbit(down, { x: 1 }));
```

---

Page: https://ratmath.com/chaos/equilibria.html

Topic

## Equilibria and their bifurcations

An equilibrium is a point where the field vanishes. Which ones exist, and whether they attract, is the skeleton of a flow, and the parameter values at which that skeleton changes are its bifurcations.

```js
const L = lorenz();
const box = { x: [-30, 30], y: [-30, 30], z: [-10, 60] };
L.equilibria(box).map((e) => e.kind);          // ["saddle-focus", "saddle", "saddle-focus"], proven to be all
L.bifurcations("r", ["1/2", 30], box);
// a pitchfork with r between 0.99999989 and 1.00000056,
// a Hopf bifurcation with r between 24.73684178 and 24.73684237   (470/19 = 24.7368421…)
```

### Finding every equilibrium

`equilibria(region)` solves f(x)=0 in a box, with a range for each variable. As for [periodic points of maps](https://ratmath.com/chaos/plane-maps.html), the box is subdivided; a piece is discarded when interval arithmetic shows that f cannot vanish on it, and kept when Krawczyk's test proves that it holds exactly one zero. The list's `complete` says that everything else was discarded, so the list is all of them.

Each equilibrium comes with the eigenvalues of the Jacobian there, as enclosures, and a `kind` read from the signs of their real parts:

- sink or spiral sink: all real parts negative; nearby orbits come in (spiralling when there is a complex pair). stability: "stable".

- source or spiral source: all positive.

- saddle or saddle-focus: some of each; unstableDimension counts the positive ones.

- undecided: an enclosure of a real part contains 0. The linearisation does not decide stability there, and the library does not guess.

That the linearisation does decide in the other cases is the Hartman–Grobman theorem: near an equilibrium with no eigenvalue on the imaginary axis, the flow looks like its linear part.

### Bifurcations

As a parameter moves, equilibria move with it, and at special values they are created, destroyed or change stability. Each of these needs an eigenvalue to cross the imaginary axis:

- Saddle-node (fold): two equilibria, one more stable than the other, collide and vanish. Normal form x′=μ−x2.

- Pitchfork: one equilibrium changes stability and throws off two new ones. Normal form x′=μx−x3; it needs a symmetry.

- Transcritical: two equilibria pass through each other and exchange stability. Normal form x′=μx−x2.

- Hopf: a complex pair crosses the axis; a spiral sink becomes a spiral source, and a periodic orbit is born or dies there.

`bifurcations(param, [from, to], region)` samples the parameter range, and at each sample proves and classifies all the equilibria. Where two neighbouring samples differ, in number or in stability after the equilibria have been paired by position, the bracket is halved, again and again, until it is narrower than `tol` (one millionth by default). The kind is read from what changed. What is certified is the two ends: at `parameter[0]` the equilibria are exactly as listed under `before`, and at `parameter[1]` as under `after`. Close to a bifurcation the proofs get harder, because that is where the Jacobian stops being invertible; if they stop succeeding before the bracket is narrow enough, the result has `stalled: true` and the wider bracket.

### The Lorenz system, as r grows

For r the origin is the only equilibrium and it attracts everything: no convection. At r=1 a pitchfork: the origin becomes a saddle and two new sinks appear at x=y=±b(r−1)​, convection rolls turning one way or the other. They are stable until

r=s−b−1s(s+b+3)​=19470​≈24.7368,
where a Hopf bifurcation makes both unstable. Beyond it no equilibrium attracts, and at r=28 the orbits wander on the strange attractor for ever. The search finds both bifurcations without being told the formula.

| call | returns |

| F.equilibria(region, { tol, maxBoxes }) | [{ point, eigenvalues, kind, stability, unstableDimension, spiral }] with .complete |

| F.bifurcations(param, [from, to], region, { samples = 24, tol }) | [{ parameter: [lo, hi], kind, before, after, stalled }] |

### Try it

```js
const show = (iv, n = 8) => iv.low.toDecimal(n);
const L = lorenz();
const box = { x: [-30, 30], y: [-30, 30], z: [-10, 60] };
const eq = L.equilibria(box);
PRINT("Lorenz at r = 28:", eq.length, "equilibria, complete:", eq.complete);
for (const e of eq) PRINT(`  (${e.point.map((x) => show(x, 6)).join(", ")})  ${e.kind}, eigenvalues ${e.eigenvalues.map((v) => v.re.low.toDecimal(4) + (v.im.high.toNumber() > 0 ? " + " + v.im.low.toDecimal(4) + "i" : v.im.low.toNumber() < 0 ? " − " + v.im.high.negate().toDecimal(4) + "i" : "")).join(", ")}`);
for (const b of L.bifurcations("r", ["1/2", 30], box)) PRINT(`  ${b.kind} for r between ${b.parameter[0].toDecimal(8)} and ${b.parameter[1].toDecimal(8)}: ${b.before.join(", ")} → ${b.after.join(", ")}`);
PRINT("470/19 =", (470 / 19).toFixed(8));
const one = (f) => flow([f], { params: { mu: 0 } }).bifurcations("mu", [-1, 1], { x: [-3, 3] })[0];
for (const f of ["mu - x^2", "mu*x - x^3", "mu*x - x^2"]) {
  const b = one(f);
  PRINT(`x′ = ${f}: ${b.kind} with μ in [${b.parameter[0].toNumber().toExponential(1)}, ${b.parameter[1].toNumber().toExponential(1)}]`);
}
const h = vanDerPol(0).bifurcations("mu", [-1, 1], { x: [-3, 3], y: [-3, 3] })[0];
PRINT(`Van der Pol: ${h.kind} at μ = 0: ${h.before} → ${h.after}`);
pendulum("1/2").equilibria({ x: [-4, 4], y: [-1, 1] }).map((e) => `${e.kind} at x = ${show(e.point[0], 10)}`)
```

---

Page: https://ratmath.com/chaos/iterated-function-systems.html

Topic

## Iterated function systems

A handful of maps that each shrink the plane determine one compact set, the attractor, that is the union of its own images. With rational coefficients its stages are exact, and its dimension is exact or proven.

```js
const S = attractors.sierpinski();          // three maps (x, y) → (x/2, y/2) + shift
S.stage(5);                                  // 243 exact rational points
S.contraction();                             // { bounds: [1/2, 1/2, 1/2], contracting: true }
S.similarityDimension();                     // log 3 / log 2, as a certified interval
S.chaosGame(20000, { seed: 7 });             // float points, kind "estimated"
new IFS([{ a: "1/3", d: "1/3" }, { a: "1/3", d: "1/3", e: "2/3" }]);   // the Cantor set on a line
```

### Hutchinson's theorem

Let f1​,…,fN​ be maps of the plane with ∣fi​(p)−fi​(q)∣≤ri​∣p−q∣ and every ri​<1. The map on compact sets F(K)=f1​(K)∪⋯∪fN​(K) is then a contraction in the Hausdorff distance, so it has exactly one fixed set A=F(A), and Fn(K)→A from any start. That set is the attractor.

Each map here is affine, (x,y)↦(ax+by+e, cx+dy+f), with rational coefficients, written as an `Affine` or as a plain object such as `{ a: "1/2", d: "1/2", e: "1/4", f: "1/2" }`. `stage(n)` applies F n times to the fixed point of the first map (which lies in A), so every point it returns is a point of the attractor, exactly.

### Is it a contraction?

The Lipschitz constant of an affine map is the largest singular value of its matrix, σ=λmax​(MTM)​, usually irrational. `contraction()` returns a rational upper bound for each map, from λmax​=2t+t2−4det2​​ with t=a2+b2+c2+d2, every square root rounded up. When all bounds are below 1 the attractor exists. The bound is exact for similarities, so the dragons' 1/2​ comes out as the rational just above it.

### Similarity dimension

When every map is a similarity with ratio ri​ (a rotation or reflection times a scale), the similarity dimension is the s with

r1s​+⋯+rNs​=1
(Moran's equation). If the pieces overlap little (the open set condition), this is also the Hausdorff dimension. With equal ratios, s=logN/log(1/r): exact when that is rational, as for the Heighway dragon (two pieces of ratio 1/2​, so s = 2), and otherwise a certified interval, as for Sierpinski's log3/log2. Unequal ratios are solved by bisection with each term enclosed, so `moran(["1/2", "1/4"])` encloses log2​φ, the golden ratio's logarithm. The open set condition is not checked.

### The chaos game, and box counting

Picking one map at random each step and applying it to a point gives points that fill the attractor (the probabilities matter for Barnsley's fern, where the stem map is chosen 1% of the time). The library seeds its own generator, so a picture can be repeated, and returns floats with `kind: "estimated"`. `boxCounting(points)` counts the boxes of side 2−k the points meet and fits a line: an estimate of the box dimension, which for Sierpinski comes out near 1.585.

| call | returns |

| new IFS(maps, { name, probabilities }) | An IFS; maps are Affine or { a, b, c, d, e, f } |

| stage(n, start), step(points), fixedPoint(i) | Exact rational points |

| contraction() | { bounds, contracting } |

| similarityDimension(), moran(ratios) | { kind: "exact" \| "certified", value, interval, formula } |

| chaosGame(n, { seed, skip }), boxCounting(points, { scales }) | Estimated: Float64Array points; { dimension, rows } |

| attractors | sierpinski, carpet, vicsek, cantorDust, heighway, levyDragon, barnsley |

### Try it

```js
const S = attractors.sierpinski();
const pts = S.stage(3);
PRINT(`stage 3 has ${pts.length} exact points, e.g.`, pts.slice(0, 4).map(([x, y]) => `(${x}, ${y})`).join(" "));
PRINT("contraction bounds:", S.contraction().bounds.join(", "));
const d = S.similarityDimension();
PRINT(`dimension ${d.formula} in [${d.interval[0].toDecimal(10)}, ${d.interval[1].toDecimal(10)}]`);
PRINT("Heighway dragon:", attractors.heighway().similarityDimension().value.toString(), "(exact)");
const g = moran(["1/2", "1/4"]);
PRINT("(1/2)^s + (1/4)^s = 1 at s ≈", g.interval[0].toDecimal(10), "  log2(golden ratio) =", Math.log2((1 + Math.sqrt(5)) / 2).toFixed(10));
// a small picture from the chaos game
const fern = attractors.barnsley().chaosGame(30000, { seed: 3 });
const W = 40, H = 24, grid = Array.from({ length: H }, () => Array(W).fill(" "));
for (let i = 0; i < fern.count; i++) {
  const x = Math.floor(((fern.points[2 * i] + 2.7) / 5.5) * W), y = H - 1 - Math.floor((fern.points[2 * i + 1] / 10.01) * H);
  if (x >= 0 && x < W && y >= 0 && y < H) grid[y][x] = "*";
}
PRINT("box dimension of the Sierpinski triangle, estimated:", boxCounting(S.chaosGame(20000)).dimension.toFixed(3));
grid.map((r) => r.join("")).join("\n")
```

---

Page: https://ratmath.com/chaos/cantor-sets.html

Topic

## Cantor sets and dimension

The middle-thirds Cantor set is the numbers in [0, 1] with a base-3 expansion using only the digits 0 and 2. Whether a fraction belongs to it is a question with a definite answer, and the library answers it exactly.

```js
const C = cantor();                         // base 3, digits 0 and 2
C.contains("1/4");                           // { inside: true, expansion: "0.#02" }: 0.020202… in base 3
C.contains("1/2");                           // { inside: false, … }
C.stage(3);                                  // the 8 intervals of the third stage, exactly
C.measure(10);                               // 1024/59049
C.dimension();                               // log 2 / log 3, certified
cantor({ base: 10, digits: [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8] });   // decimals without a 9
```

### Membership is decidable

x is in the set exactly when some allowed digit d leaves 3x−d in [0, 1] and in the set again. For a rational x=n/D every number reached this way has the same denominator D, and there are only D + 1 such numbers in [0, 1]. So the steps form a finite graph, and x is in the set exactly when the graph has an infinite path from x, which means a path that reaches a cycle. `contains` searches for one and returns the repeating expansion it found. A number can have two expansions (1/3 is 0.1000… and also 0.0222…), and the search finds the allowed one when there is one.

The answer is not a matter of precision. 1/4 is in the Cantor set although it is never an end point of a removed interval, and 1/2 is not, although every stage contains points as close to it as you like.

### Stages, measure and dimension

Stage n is the union of kn intervals of length b−n, where k is the number of allowed digits; touching intervals are merged. The total length is (k/b)n, which tends to 0 whenever a digit is missing, so the set has measure zero. Its dimension is logk/logb: the set is made of k copies of itself scaled by 1/b. That is exact when rational (base 4 with two digits gives 1/2) and a certified interval otherwise.

The expansion of any rational in any base, with its repeating part marked by `#`, comes from Core: `C.expansion("1/4")`.

| call | returns |

| cantor({ base = 3, digits = [0, 2] }) | A DigitCantor |

| contains(q) | { inside, expansion?, reason } |

| expansion(q) | Core's base-b expansion, with # before the repeating part |

| stage(n), measure(n) | [lo, hi] rational pairs; (k/b)^n |

| dimension() | { kind, value, interval, formula } |

### Try it

```js
const C = cantor();
for (const q of ["1/4", "3/4", "1/3", "1/10", "1/2", "9/13", "1/13"]) {
  const r = C.contains(q);
  PRINT(q.padEnd(5), r.inside ? `inside, base 3 ${r.expansion}` : "not inside", "   Core:", C.expansion(q));
}
PRINT("stage 2:", C.stage(2).map(([a, b]) => `[${a}, ${b}]`).join(" "));
PRINT("measure of stage 20:", C.measure(20).toString());
const d = C.dimension();
PRINT("dimension", d.formula, "≈", d.interval[0].toDecimal(12));
// fractions with denominator below 30 that lie in the set
const found = [];
for (let D = 2; D < 30; D++) for (let n = 1; n < D; n++) if (C.contains(`${n}/${D}`).inside && gcd(n, D) === 1) found.push(`${n}/${D}`);
function gcd(a, b) { return b ? gcd(b, a % b) : a; }
found.join(" ")
```

---

Page: https://ratmath.com/chaos/l-systems.html

Topic

## L-systems

An L-system rewrites every symbol of a string at once, then a turtle draws the result. The strings grow exponentially, but how many of each symbol they hold is a matrix power, exact for any n, and for angles that are multiples of 30° every point the turtle visits is exactly a + b√3.

```js
const K = lsystems.koch();                  // axiom F, F → F+F--F+F, angle 60°
K.generate(2);                               // the string after two rewritings
K.counts(100).counts.F;                      // 4^100, exactly, without writing the string
K.turtle(3).exactSegments;                   // end points as Q3 numbers a + b√3
lsystem({ axiom: "X", rules: { X: "F+[[X]-X]-F[-FX]+X", F: "FF" }, angle: 25 });
```

### Parallel rewriting

An L-system has an axiom and rules mapping single symbols to strings; symbols without a rule are copied. One step rewrites every symbol at the same time. Lindenmayer used them for the growth of plants, where every cell divides at once. `generate(n)` writes the string out, refusing past five million symbols.

### Counting without writing

Let Mab​ be the number of b in the rule for a. If v counts the symbols of the axiom, then vMn counts the symbols after n steps, and repeated squaring gives Mn with BigInt entries in about log2​n multiplications. For the Koch curve M has the eigenvalue 4, so the curve has 4n segments, each 3−n long: its length (4/3)n grows without bound while it stays in a bounded region. For the dragon the counts follow powers of 2.

### The turtle, exactly

F and G draw a unit step, f moves without drawing, + and − turn by the angle, | turns around, and [ ] save and restore the position and heading. When the angle is a multiple of 30°, cos and sin of every heading are among 0,±21​,±1,±23​​, so every position is a+b3​ with rational a and b. The library carries those as `Q3` numbers, which is how it can say the Koch snowflake closes up exactly: its end point is (0, 0), not something within 10⁻¹⁵ of it. Other angles (the 25° plant, the 45° Lévy curve) are drawn in floats and the result says `kind: "float"`.

| call | returns |

| lsystem({ axiom, rules, angle, draw = "FG", move = "f" }) | An LSystem |

| generate(n) | The string |

| counts(n) | { counts: { symbol: BigInt }, length: BigInt } |

| turtle(n, { step }) | { kind, segments, exactSegments, end } |

| lsystems | koch, snowflake, arrowhead, dragon, hilbert, levy, plant |

| Q3 | a + b√3: add, mul, equals, toNumber, toString |

### Try it

```js
const K = lsystems.koch();
PRINT("after 2 steps:", K.generate(2));
const c = K.counts(60);
PRINT("after 60 steps: F appears", c.counts.F.toString(), "times; length", c.length.toString());
const S = lsystems.snowflake().turtle(2);
PRINT("snowflake, stage 2:", S.segments.length, "segments, ends at (", S.end.map(String).join(", "), ")");
PRINT("a corner of it:", S.exactSegments[5].slice(2).map(String).join(", "));
// draw the Hilbert curve on a character grid
const H = lsystems.hilbert().turtle(3);
const n = 8, grid = Array.from({ length: 2 * n - 1 }, () => Array(2 * n - 1).fill(" "));
for (const [x1, y1, x2, y2] of H.segments) {
  const [a, b, c2, d] = [x1, y1, x2, y2].map((v) => Math.round(v));
  grid[2 * n - 2 - (b + d)][a + c2] = a === c2 ? "|" : "-";
  grid[2 * n - 2 - 2 * b][2 * a] = "o";
  grid[2 * n - 2 - 2 * d][2 * c2] = "o";
}
grid.map((r) => r.join("")).join("\n")
```

---

Page: https://ratmath.com/chaos/cellular-automata.html

Topic

## Cellular automata

Cells that are 0 or 1, updated by a local rule: the discrete end of dynamics, where everything is exact and yet rule 30 looks random and Life can compute anything.

```js
elementary(90).fromCell(15);                // rows of Pascal's triangle mod 2
elementary(110).equivalents;                 // [110, 124, 137, 193]
elementary(184).cycle("10101010");           // { transient: 0, period: 2 }
life(patterns.glider).classify();            // { kind: "spaceship", period: 4, speed: "c/4", … }
life("OOO\nO..\nO..", { rule: "B36/S23" }); // HighLife
```

### Elementary rules

A row of cells, each new cell determined by itself and its two neighbours. There are 23=8 neighbourhoods and so 28=256 rules, numbered by Wolfram: bit n of the rule number is the new cell for the neighbourhood whose binary value is n. Reflecting left and right, or swapping 0 and 1, turns one rule into another that behaves the same way, which cuts 256 rules to 88 classes; `equivalents` lists a rule's class.

Rule 90 is additive: the new cell is the sum mod 2 of the two neighbours. From one live cell, row t is then the binomial coefficients (kt​) mod 2, which is Sierpinski's triangle again, and by Lucas's theorem (kt​) is odd exactly when the binary digits of k are a subset of those of t. `additive` tests the linearity condition directly and finds exactly the eight rules 0, 60, 90, 102, 150, 170, 204, 240.

On a ring of n cells there are 2n rows, so every orbit eventually repeats; `cycle` finds when and with what period. Rule 30 from one cell looks random enough that its centre column was used as a random number generator, and rule 110 was proved capable of universal computation.

### Life

Conway's Game of Life on the unbounded plane: a dead cell with exactly 3 live neighbours is born, a live one with 2 or 3 survives. Other rules are written the same way, as "B3/S23". Only live cells are stored, so a glider can travel forever.

`classify` runs a pattern and compares each generation's shape, moved to the origin, with all earlier ones, cell by cell. A repeat in the same place is a still life or an oscillator with that period; a repeat that has moved is a spaceship, with its speed in cells per generation as a fraction of c, the speed of light (one cell per step). The glider moves one cell diagonally every 4 generations, c/4; the lightweight spaceship moves 2 cells in 4, c/2. Patterns that grow forever, like the Gosper glider gun, never repeat and come back as "unknown" within the limit.

| call | returns |

| elementary(rule) | Elementary: table, mirror, complement, equivalents, additive |

| step(row, { boundary }), run(initial, steps), fromCell(steps) | Uint8Array rows |

| cycle(initial, { limit }) | { transient, period } |

| showRows(rows, on, off) | Rows as text |

| life(cells, { rule }) | Life: population, step(), run(n), bounds(), classify(), toString() |

| patterns | block, blinker, toad, beacon, glider, lwss, pulsar, rpentomino, gosperGun |

### Try it

```js
PRINT(showRows(elementary(90).fromCell(15)));
PRINT("");
PRINT(showRows(elementary(30).fromCell(15)));
PRINT("rule 30 is equivalent to", elementary(30).equivalents.join(", "));
PRINT("additive rules:", Array.from({ length: 256 }, (_, r) => r).filter((r) => elementary(r).additive).join(", "));
for (const name of ["block", "blinker", "pulsar", "glider", "lwss"]) {
  const c = life(patterns[name]).classify();
  PRINT(name.padEnd(8), c.kind, c.period ?? "", c.speed ?? "");
}
const r = life(patterns.rpentomino);
PRINT("R-pentomino: population after 100 generations", r.run(100).population);
life(patterns.glider).run(4).toString()
```

---

Page: https://ratmath.com/chaos/mandelbrot-and-julia.html

Topic

## Mandelbrot and Julia sets

A pixel is a small square of the plane, not a point. Here every pixel of a Mandelbrot or Julia picture is proved to lie outside the set, proved to lie inside it, or left undecided, and only the boundary is ever undecided.

```js
mandelbrot({ re: ["-2", "1/2"], im: ["-5/4", "5/4"], width: 72, height: 30 });
julia("-1", { re: ["-2", "2"], im: ["-1", "1"] });   // the basilica
mandelbrotPoint("-13/10");                   // { verdict: "inside", period: 4, … }
juliaPoint("-1", "1/2");                     // an exact z₀ under z → z² − 1
```

### The sets

For fc​(z)=z2+c, the filled Julia set Kc​ is the set of z whose orbit stays bounded, and the Mandelbrot set M is the set of c for which the orbit of 0 stays bounded. Both are compact, and the usual pictures colour a point by how many steps its float orbit takes to pass 2. That is a heuristic twice over: the point stands for a whole pixel, and the float orbit is not the true orbit.

### Outside, proved

If ∣z∣>max(2,∣c∣) then ∣fc​(z)∣>∣z∣, and the orbit goes to infinity. The library carries the whole pixel as a box of complex numbers in interval arithmetic, with every float result moved outward by more than its rounding error, so if some iterate of the box lies entirely beyond the radius, every point of the pixel escapes.

### Inside, proved

Being inside is harder, because no finite number of steps shows that an orbit stays bounded forever. Two tests prove it here. For M, the main cardioid q(q+x−41​)<4y2​ with q=(x−41​)2+y2, and the disc (x+1)2+y2<161​, contain exactly the c with an attracting fixed point or 2-cycle; the inequalities are checked on the whole pixel. Otherwise the library looks for a trap: a box B around the orbit's current position with fp(B)⊂B in intervals. Then every later iterate stays in B, so the orbit is bounded, and B holds an attracting cycle of period dividing p. A pixel that cannot be decided whole is split into 4, then 16 pieces (`depth`).

For Julia sets the trap is built around the attracting cycle (found in floats, then proved by the trap itself). If fc​ has no attracting cycle, as for c outside M, nothing can be inside and nothing is claimed.

### Single points, exactly

`mandelbrotPoint(c)` and `juliaPoint(c, z0)` do the same for one exact point with the complex package's rational rectangles, rounded outward to a chosen number of bits. Points on the boundary, such as c=41​, −43​ or −2, stay undecided, which is the honest answer: they are in M, but no escape or trap argument shows it.

| call | returns |

| mandelbrot({ re, im, width, height, maxIter, maxPeriod, depth }) | PixelGrid: kind (0 undecided, 1 inside, 2 outside), counts, escape, toText() |

| julia(c, { re, im, width, height, maxIter, depth }) | PixelGrid, with the cycle it trapped |

| mandelbrotPoint(c, { maxIter, bits, maxPeriod }) | { verdict, reason, period? or escape? } |

| juliaPoint(c, z0, { … }) | The same for a point of the plane |

### Try it

```js
const M = mandelbrot({ width: 60, height: 24, maxIter: 120 });
PRINT(M.toText("?█ "));
PRINT(String(M));
for (const c of ["0", "-1", "-13/10", "-0.12 + 0.75i", "1/2", "1/4", "-2"]) {
  const v = mandelbrotPoint(c, { maxIter: 300 });
  PRINT(c.padEnd(14), v.verdict.padEnd(10), v.reason);
}
const J = julia("-1", { width: 60, height: 16, re: ["-2", "2"], im: ["-1", "1"] });
PRINT(J.toText("?█ "));
String(J)
```

---

Page: https://ratmath.com/chaos/newton-basins.html

Topic

## Newton basins

Newton's method for z³ − 1 sends almost every starting point to one of the three cube roots of 1, but the boundaries between the three basins are fractal: at every point of the boundary all three basins meet.

```js
newtonBasins(["1", "0", "0", "-1"]);        // z³ − 1: three labelled basins
newtonBasins(["1", "0", "-1"], { width: 40, height: 20 });   // z² − 1: two half-planes
newtonBasins(["1", "0", "1", "0", "-1"]);   // z⁴ + z² − 1, coefficients highest first
```

### Newton's map

For a polynomial p, Newton's method iterates N(z)=z−p(z)/p′(z). Near a simple root it converges quadratically, but far from the roots the behaviour is a dynamical system in its own right. Cayley asked in 1879 which root a starting point goes to; for z2−1 the answer is the nearer one, and for z3−1 the boundary of each basin is the boundary of all three, a Julia set of the rational map N.

### What is proved

For each root the library builds a small box B around a float approximation and checks, in interval arithmetic, that N(B)⊂B. By Brouwer's theorem N then has a fixed point in B, which is a root of p, and since B is small enough that ∣N′∣<1 there, every point of B goes to that root. The image is computed with the mean-value form

N(Z)⊆N(m)+N′(Z)(Z−m),N′=(p′)2pp′′​,
where m is the centre of the box; evaluating N directly on a box loses too much to the dependency problem. A pixel gets label k when its interval Newton orbit enters the k-th proved box, so every point of the pixel converges to root k. Pixels are split up to `depth` times when the whole cannot be followed. Boundary pixels, and pixels near a critical point of p where p′ vanishes, stay undecided.

Coefficients are exact (complex ones written `"1/2 + 3i"`). A root that could not be proved, a multiple root for instance, is listed under `unproved` and its basin is not labelled.

| call | returns |

| newtonBasins(coefficients, { re, im, width, height, maxIter, depth }) | PixelGrid: kind (0 undecided, k for root k), roots (with their proved boxes), unproved, counts |

### Try it

```js
const G = newtonBasins(["1", "0", "0", "-1"], { width: 60, height: 24, re: ["-2", "2"], im: ["-3/2", "3/2"] });
PRINT(G.toText("?abc"));
PRINT(String(G));
G.roots.forEach((r, k) => PRINT(`root ${k + 1} (${"abc"[k]}): in [${r.re[0].toFixed(12)}, ${r.re[1].toFixed(12)}] + i[${r.im[0].toFixed(12)}, ${r.im[1].toFixed(12)}]`));
const two = newtonBasins(["1", "0", "-1"], { width: 40, height: 8 });
PRINT("z² − 1: roots", two.roots.map((r, k) => `${k + 1} near ${r.approx[0].toFixed(6)}`).join(", "));
two.toText("?12")
```
